data.text: Founding
One man's gift shaped this community treasure. Richard Stanhope Pullen donated farmland in 1887 for the park that bears his name.

Richard Stanhope Pullen gave North Carolina its first public park. After New York City's Central Park opened as the nation's first public park in 1876, R.S. Pullen decided that Raleigh needed a park of its own. City planners of the time knew that nature parks gave the physical and mental refreshment that is vital to community growth.
In 1889, R.S. Pullen, along with Wiley Howell, the park keeper, and Washington Ligon transplanted one thousand trees and planted flowers to transform the former cow pasture into Pullen Park.

data.caption: Article from News and Observer, December 5th, 1886. This park officially opened to the public in the Spring of 1888

data.text: A path around the pond allowed guests to stroll by or stop to admire the goldfish. The pond was enlarged into a lake during the park's expansion in 1835.

R.S. Pullen had big dreams for Raleigh. Pullen knew that the park would attract new businesses to Raleigh - and he was right. In 1887, the park was outside the city limits, but now it is near the heart of the Capital's downtown district. Thanks to the forethought of one man, Pullen Park has enriched the lives of Raleigh citizens for over 100 years.

data.caption: Photograph taken by Patrick Sheehan

data.text: The deed for the land States that it was given as “a Public Park to be used perpetually for the recreation and pleasures of the inhabitants of the City of Raleigh.”
First in North Carolina. Pullen Park has the honor of being the state's first public park. It is also the fiftholdest operating amusement park in the United States and the 16th-oldest in the world.

The park is the best-known of Pullen's gifts to Raleigh. R.S. Pullen was known as Raleigh's greatest philanthropist, but we remember him most for Pullen Park. After giving the city the land, Pullen used his own money to build the park's pool, pavilion, bathhouse, and lily pond. He also built roads and bridges to the park and provided land for college that is now named North Carolina State University.

Pullen stayed out of the spotlight. You won't see a statue honoring R.S. Pullen for his role in recreating this park. He shunned formal recognition and even refused to have his photograph taken. That did not keep him, however, from remaining actively involved in the park until his death in 1895. Today, a small plaque at the Pullen Aquatic Center honors his many contributions.

data.caption: Courtesy of The Louise Round Wilson Special Collections Library

data.text: R.S. Pullen helped finance a trolley to bring people to the park. When Pullen Park first opened, it was a mile from the city center. Guests came on foot, and mule-drawn carriages, or they wrote rode a trolley (as shown above). It is remembered that, even then, the park's crowds created traffic jams - but with carriages instead of cars. On Sundays, family strolled, picnicked, and socialized in the popular park.
Hey Kids! Parks are places to relax in nature and have fun. If you were building a park today, what features would you include?

data.caption: Courtesy of State Archives of North Carolina

data.text: A city in need of a park. A map of Raleigh in 1872 shows a cluster of buildings but few natural spaces intended for relaxation and recreation.
Swim
The Pullen Park pool was the best part of summer in Raleigh. Raleigh's first public swimming pool opened here in 1862.

The original “bathing pool” was constructed entirely of wood. The Pullen Park “bathing pool” (below) was built in 1892. A stream supplied the water which, in turn, filtered back into the ground through cracks in the wood. The City updated the pool to concrete in 1913. This allowed for the use of chlorine to purify the water.

data.caption: Courtesy State Archives of North Carolina, ca. 1912.

data.text: The pool was originally open only to males - who “bathed” unclothed. Later, in 1895, the pool opened two days a week for “females only” who wore bathing suits.

data.caption: Courtesy of Library of Congress
Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art

data.text: Early female swimsuits reflected modesty at the turn of the century. In the 1890s, female “bathing suits” were made of wool and cotton. A 1920s suit shows a looser fitting suit that allowed the arms to show. While not functional, the outfits achieve their purpose: to conceal a woman's body.
After swimming became an Olympic sport in 1896, people saw that women’s swimsuits needed to be streamlined and less heavy. This paved the way for modern women's swimwear.

data.caption: State Archives of North Carolina, ca 1950.

data.text: Segregation was challenged at the pool. For decades, only whites were allowed to swim at Pullen Park. That changed in 1962 when a group of African American and white students entered the pool together.

data.caption: Image courtesy of News and Observer, August 7, 1962

data.text: The park's original swimming pool was replaced in 1935. The Works Progress Administration (WPA) employed Americans during the Great Depression. The WPA built a new pool and a bathhouse with a dance hall upstairs (left) in Pullen Park. This pool was demolished 1992 when the new Aquatic Center was built. After 2018 renovations, Pullen Aquatic Center (below) boasts an indoor Olympic-size swimming pool - which is twice the size of the original Pullen Park pool. Today, the center offers swimming lessons, water aerobics, an intra-city swim team, and is used for regional swimming competitions.
Hey Kids! Over the years, thousands of children have learned to swim at Pullen Park. If you want to learn, you can take lessons at Pullen Aquatic Center.
Segregation
Pullen Park’s pool embodied the quest for racial equality. Raleigh's public pools were integrated during the Civil Rights Movement.

An 1896 ruling allowed racial segregation in public areas. With Plessy v. Ferguson, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed public places to be segregated by race as long as there was a “separate but equal alternative.” In response, Jim Crow laws were put in place throughout the South. The term “Jim Crow” referred to a black face minstrel character, and the name was used to describe state and local laws that legalized segregation. As a result of Jim Crow laws, African Americans experienced discrimination in most public places, including restaurants, hospitals, transportation, theatres, hotels, and parks.

data.caption: Courtesy of News and Observer, May 18, 1954.

data.text: When did segregation end? A breakthrough occurred when school segregation was banned in 1954 (above). In 1864, the Civil Rights Act legally ended racial segregation. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968 prohibited voting and housing discrimination based on race.

Sit-ins were a non-violent way to challenge segregation. In February 1960, four African American students - later known as the Greensboro Four - sat down at a “white's-only” lunch counter at a Woolsworth’s in Greensboro, NC, where they asked to be served. This non-violent action was critical turning point in the Civil Rights Movement. Within a week, students in other cities - including Raleigh - began similar sit-ins. Picketers asked for a boycott of the stores and it worked. Six months after the sitins began, lunch counters at Woolsworth’s stores were integrated.

data.caption: John Chavis Memorial Park was built with WPA funding in 1937 as a “separate but equal” park for African Americans. The park featured a pool, carousel, and other amusements. Courtesy of News and Observer, February 10, 1960.

Days after the Greensboro Four protest, students staged a sit-in at a Raleigh Woolsworth’s in a nonviolent protest against racially segregated lunch counters. Courtesy of News and Observer, February 16, 1960
Protesters strike outside on Fayetteville street in downtown Raleigh because of racial discrimination.

data.text: Students peacefully protested the segregated pool at Pullen Park. During the Jim Crow era, while not an official rule, people of different races could not swim together at Pullen Park. In 1962, a group of African Americans and white students defied the practice and swam together (left and right). The City of Raleigh responded by closing the pools at Pullen Park and John Chavis Memorial Park.

data.caption: On August 6th, 1962, Percy High is seen leaving the Pullen Park pool as City Recreation Director Jimmy Chambers looks on. Photo courtesy of News and Observer, August 7, 1962.
Percy High, Gary Perry, Jimmy Thorpe, and Tracy Rogers attempted a peaceful act to integrate the Pullen Park pool on August 6, 1862. Courtesy of News and Observer, August 7, 1962

data.text: Raleigh's pools were integrated in 1963. As the quest for civil rights swept the nation, many cities, including Raleigh, resisted integration by closing pools. Other cities created private pool clubs and charged a fee to join. With any year, however, Raleigh's City Council voted in favor of integrating the pools at Pullen Park and Chavis Park. This brought an end to 67 years of legal segregation Raleigh's parks.

data.caption: Article from The Charlotte Observer, Feb. 5, 1963.

data.text: Hey Kids! Ask your parents or grandparents to share their memories of swimming at Pullen Park or Chavis Park when they were kids.

Pullen Park is for everyone. Today, people of every age, race, identity, and income level come to Pullen Park. Here they swim, play, relax, exercise, picnic, or simply enjoy nature. Parks are an asset for our diverse and growing community.
Zoo
Pullen Park's zoo was the star attraction in the early 1900s. The small collection began with two raccoons and later grew to over 200 animals.

Zoos in public parks were all the rage in the late 1800s. It all began with the opening of the nation’s first zoo in Philadelphia’s Fairmount Park in 1874. Raleigh followed this national trend by adding a small zoo to Pullen Park in 1899. Although rustic by today’s standards, the zoo drew massive crowds eager to see the exotic animals up close.

data.caption: Image of the Pullen Park zoo enclosures from a brochure published in 1904 by the Raleigh Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

data.text: The park's keeper cared for every animal. Wiley Howell served as the Park Keeper from 1888 to 1936. He took care of zoo animals like Belle the lioness and Jim the buffalo, plus creatures such as alligators, bears, monkeys, and others.

data.caption: From the Technician, the student newspaper at North Carolina State University, August 28, 1985.

data.text: Pullen Park visitors often mistreated the animals. While the zoo was an operation, it was common for guests to taunt the animals, as well as feed them unhealthy food. It was a constant challenge for park staff to repair damaged enclosures and protect the animals, such as Jim the buffalo (above), from visitor's actions.

data.caption: Courtesy of Raleigh Magazine, 1970.

data.text: Hey Kids! The photos at right showed some of the animals that lived at the Pullen Park zoo. Ask a friend if they can name them.
Answers:
Top row: Squirrel monkey, Wolf, Australian masked owl, Raccoon;
Second row: Rabbit, Bald eagle, Red fox, American alligator;
Third row: Male peafowl (often called a peacock), American black bear, Canada goose, African lion.
The first animals purchased for the zoo included raccoons, rabbits, guinea pigs, and a monkey. Jim the buffalo and Belle the lioness were donated to the zoo by a travelling circus.

data.caption: Courtesy of North Carolina Zoo.

data.text: The Pullen Park zoo closed in 1941. The zoo declined after the death of Park Keeper Wiley Howell in 1936. In 1941, the zoo closed after Hoover the bear died, leaving just a few animals left on display. The city temporarily reopened the zoo in 1963 with a monkey and a fox. There was no longer a need for local zoo when the North Carolina Zoo opened in Asheboro, NC, in 1974.

Today’s zoos are refugees for wildlife. Modern zoos meet the animals’ physical, social, in psychological needs with state-of-the-art design, care and accommodations. Visitors stand in awe of wild creatures from around the globe. For many rare species, zoos are the last hope for survival.
Carousel
This carousel has created generations of smiles. Pullen Park welcomed this community treasure in 1921.

The Pullen Park Dentzel Carousel is a historical gem. For more than 100 years, families have flocked to Pullen Park to ride the carousel. This attraction was built in 1911 by Gustav Dentzel of Germantown, Pennsylvania. The carousel remains one of the most popular attractions in the park. Over 250,000 guests take a spin on it every year.

data.caption: Courtesy of State Archives of North Carolina, ca. 1913.

data.text: Carousels have been at Pullen Park since 1906. The Dentzel Carousel, originally located at nearby Bloomsbury Park (above), was not the first carousel at Pullen Park. The earliest carousel opened in 1906, followed by a steam powered version in 1915. Today, Pullen Park is committed to sustaining this local treasure for generations to come.

data.caption: News and Observer, May 21, 1921.
Photograph taken by Lynn Rock, August 8, 1998.

data.text: There are only a dozen or so Dentzel Carousels left in the U.S. Pullen park has one of the oldest and one of the best preserved Dentzel Carousels still in operation. Each of the 52 solid wood animals were hand-carved and expertly painted with elaborate designs.

data.caption: A volunteer restores a Pullen Park carousel horse in 1980.

data.text: The community began a five-year restoration of the carousel in 1977. Organizations and individuals including the Raleigh Fine Arts Society, Raleigh Parks and Recreation Department, conservator Rosa Patton, and many volunteers from the local arts community-raised the funds for the restoration project. Broken parts were replaced and drawings (shown at far right) were used to restore the animals' brilliant colors. The City enclosed the carousel in 2011 to protect it from future damage.
The carousel is important to Raleigh and its citizens. The Dentzel Carousel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976 and is also a designated Raleigh Historic Landmark.
Hey Kids! Just imagine… If your parents or grandparents grew up in Raleigh, they may have happy memories of riding this same carousel. Ask them which animal was their favorite to ride.
Pullen park strives to approve ADA accommodations for our guests. In 2021, a wheelchair accessible chariot joined the menagerie!

Our carousel organ plays “the happiest music on Earth.” The “happy” music comes from a #125 band organ, first installed in 1924. Created to stimulate the sound of a small brass band, the instrument is said to elevate the listener's mood.

data.caption: This drawing was used during the restoration to ensure that the animals have the proper colors.

data.text: Lake Howell
Lake Howell is the centerpiece of Pullen Park. The Lake is Raleigh's gathering spot for outdoor family fun.

President Franklin Roosevelt's “New Deal” helped to build Lake Howell. Millions were jobless during the Great Depression of the 1930s. In response, Roosevelt created the Works Progress Administration (WPA) as part of the “New Deal.” The WPA hired laborers, stonemasons, carpenters, and artisans to improve public spaces nationwide.

The WPA invested $150,000 to improve Pullen Park. That amount would be more than two million dollars today. WPA crews built the lake and expanded the swimming pool and bathhouse in the 1930s (right). The second floor of the bathhouse included a dance pavilion that later doubled as a roller skating rink. The WPA improvements made the park even more popular for family seeking outdoor fun.

data.caption: Courtesy of the State Archives of North Carolina, January, 1943.
Photo courtesy of visitraleigh.com

data.text: First it was a pond. One of the first attractions built in Pullen Park was a lily pond filled with goldfish. During the WPA expansion, the pond was enlarged to become Lake Howell. Families have long enjoyed an afternoon at Lake Howell.
An island and two bridges were added in the 1950s. Strolling and picnicking around the lake has long been popular.

data.caption: Courtesy of the State Archives of North Carolina, January, 1939.

data.text: A frozen Lake is perfect for skating. In 1939, Lake Howell frozen opened for ice skating, making it the first public ice skating rank in Raleigh. The lake was also used for ice skating when it froze in 1941.

data.caption: Article courtesy of News and Observer, January 28, 1941

data.text: The lake honors Wylie Howell, the park's first manager. For 48 years, Wylie Howell was “Keeper of the Park.” He planted trees and flowers alongside the park's founder, R.S. Pullen. Howell served as guard, manager, repairman, gardener, and zookeeper. The city memorialized his service at the park by naming the lake in his honor in 1935. At his death in 1936, he was Raleigh's Superintendent of parks.

data.caption: Image courtesy of News and Observer, June 21, 1935

data.text: Hey Kids! Can you name them? A lot of animals live in or near the lake. Ask a friend how many they can name. Here are a few: Great blue heron, Mallard duck, Canada goose, Muskrat, Largemouth bass, Northern water snake, Yellow-bellied slider turtle, and Flathead catfish.
